title: Learn German A1 in 25 Minutes (no boring grammar)

lines.say: Most German courses take an hour to teach you hello. Let's do A1 basics in 25 minutes.
Greetings, introducing yourself, numbers, ordering coffee, finding the train, and the mistakes that make Germans laugh.
Here's how it works. When you see this, repeat after me. Out loud. Yes, really.
And every noun gets a color. Blue for der, red for die, green for das.
Stay for the speed quiz at the end.
Ready? I'm your German friend, and this is Fast German. German in seconds, not hours.
First word. The easiest one in the whole language.
Same as English, just with a cleaner 'a'. Now the time-of-day greetings.
In the morning, you say Guten Morgen.
During the day, Guten Tag. Perfect for shops and offices.
In the evening, Guten Abend.
And before bed: Gute Nacht. Notice, it's gute, not guten. Little detail, big win.
Bonus! In the north, people say Moin. In the south and Austria, Servus or Grüß Gott.
Now, how are you? With friends: Wie geht's?
The answer you'll use ninety percent of the time: Gut, danke. Und dir?
Having a so-so day? Es geht. It literally means 'it goes'. Very German. Very honest.
Time to leave. Casual goodbye: Tschüss.
Formal goodbye: Auf Wiedersehen. Literally, 'until we see again'.
And the handy ones: Bis später, bis morgen, bis bald.

card.de: Bis später · Bis morgen · Bis bald

lines.say: Let's hear it in action. Two friends meet on the street.
Hallo! Wie geht's? Gut, danke. Und dir? Auch gut! Bis später! Tschüss!
Auch gut means 'also good'. Six seconds, one full conversation. You're already doing it.
Quick check. No peeking.

lines.quiz: How do you say: good evening?

lines.say: Nailed it? Great. Next, you're going to introduce yourself in three sentences.
Germans don't really say 'my name is'. They say Ich heiße. I am called.
Swap in your own name. Say it out loud. Ich heiße... you!
You can also say Ich bin Anna. I am Anna. Short, friendly, and totally normal.
To ask someone casually: Wie heißt du?
Sentence two. Where you're from: Ich komme aus.
Ich komme aus Kanada. Ich komme aus Indien. Easy. One trap: for the USA, it's aus den USA.
And the question: Woher kommst du? Where do you come from?
Sentence three. Where you live: Ich wohne in.
Question version: Wo wohnst du?
Bonus line that makes Germans smile instantly:
And when you meet someone: Freut mich! Nice to meet you.
Let's put it all together. Listen to the rhythm.
Hallo! Ich heiße Anna. Ich komme aus England, und ich wohne in Berlin. Freut mich!
Now pause the video and do yours. I'll wait. Okay, I won't. But you should.

lines.quiz: How do you say: I live in Berlin?

lines.say: Next up: the trick that makes der, die, das finally make sense.
In German, every noun has a gender. Der, die, or das. And here's the secret: it's often not logical.
So don't learn 'table'. Learn 'der Tisch'. Article plus noun, always together. That's why we use colors.
Blue is der.
Red is die.
Green is das.
Picture the color when you hear the word. Your brain loves colors. Watch the screen and let the color stick.
Here's why this matters. Germans will understand you with the wrong article. But the right one makes you sound fluent, fast. Let's do more.
Now, the weird one. Girl is neuter. Das Mädchen.
Why? Every word ending in -chen is das. Grammar beats biology here.
Two more shortcuts. Words ending in -ung, -heit, or -keit are always die. Die Zeitung. Die Freiheit.
And many words ending in -e are die too. Die Lampe. Die Tasche. Not all, but a lot.
Now, 'a' or 'an'. For der and das words, it's ein. For die words, it's eine.
See? Red words get the extra 'e'. Eine. Quick quiz. Which color?
If you got both, you're already ahead of most beginners. Now, let's count. And there's a twist at twenty-one.
Zero to five. Repeat after me.

card.de: null · eins · zwei · drei · vier · fünf

lines.repeat: null, eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf

lines.say: Six to ten.
Phone tip! On the phone, Germans often say zwo instead of zwei. Why? So it doesn't sound like drei.
Eleven and twelve are special. Elf and zwölf. Yes, elf. Like the little fantasy guy.
Thirteen to nineteen are easy: number plus zehn. Drei plus zehn is dreizehn.
Watch out for two. Sechzehn loses the s. Siebzehn loses the -en.
Now, the famous German twist. After twenty, you say the numbers backwards.
Twenty-one is 'one and twenty'. Einundzwanzig.
Like the old English nursery rhyme. Four and twenty blackbirds. German just never stopped.
The tens: dreißig, vierzig, fünfzig. Then sechzig, siebzig, achtzig, neunzig. And hundert.
So forty-five? Five and forty. Fünfundvierzig.
Your turn.
And now, how old are you? Ich bin plus your age, plus Jahre alt.
Notice that little word: bin. It's from the most important verb in German. Which brings us to the top ten.
Ten verbs. Just two forms each: ich, meaning I, and du, meaning you, casual.
Good news first. Most verbs follow one pattern. Ich ends in -e. Du ends in -st.
Number one, sein. To be. It's irregular, so just memorize it.

card.en: to be: I am · you are

lines.say: Number two, haben. To have.
Number three, gehen. To go, on foot.
Four, kommen. To come. You already know it from Ich komme aus.
Five, machen. To make or do. Was machst du? What are you doing?
Six, sprechen. To speak. Careful, the vowel changes for du: sprichst.
Seven, essen. To eat. Du isst. Two s's, one sound.
Eight, trinken. To drink. Totally regular.
Nine, möchten. Would like. The most polite verb you'll ever need.

lines.en: I would like, you would like

lines.say: Ten, können. Can. Ich kann, du kannst.
Now, real sentences. Ich habe Hunger.
Germans don't 'are' hungry. They 'have' hunger. Same with thirst: Ich habe Durst.
Now listen to how far ten verbs get you. A tiny story.
Ich bin Tom. Ich komme aus Kanada. Ich habe einen Hund. Ich spreche ein bisschen Deutsch, und ich trinke gern Kaffee.
Gern after a verb means you like doing it. Ich trinke gern Kaffee. I like drinking coffee. Handy, right?

lines.quiz: How do you say: you speak, casual?

lines.say: Ten verbs, done. That's the engine of the language. Now let's ask questions.
Most question words start with W. And the W sounds like an English V. Ready?
Wer. Who.
Was. What.
Wo. Where.
Wann. When.
Wie. How.
Warum. Why.
And two you already met. Woher, where from. And wie viel, how much. You'll use that one in every shop.
Careful! Wer is who, and wo is where. It feels backwards. Say it with me.
Here's the only rule you need. W-word first, verb second.
And for yes or no questions? Just put the verb first. That's it.
Du sprichst Englisch. You speak English. Sprichst du Englisch? Do you speak English?
Perfect. Now you can ask things. Let's use that where it matters most. Food.
You walk in. The waiter looks at you. Here's your script.
First, a table for two: Einen Tisch für zwei, bitte.
Ask for the menu: Die Speisekarte, bitte.
Now the magic phrase. Ich hätte gern. I would like to have. Super polite, super natural.
Tiny bonus rule. When you order, blue der-words switch from ein to einen. Red and green stay the same.
Germany tip: water usually comes sparkling. Want still water? Ohne Kohlensäure.
Feeling bold? Ein Bier, bitte. Das Bier, so it's green.
And when the food arrives, Germans say Guten Appetit. When glasses clink: Prost!
Delicious? One word: Lecker!
Time to pay. In Germany, the waiter won't bring the bill until you ask. So ask.
Or the very German shortcut: Zahlen, bitte. Literally, 'pay, please'.
The waiter will ask: Zusammen oder getrennt? Together or separate? Germans split bills all the time.
Some places are still cash only. So check first.
Tipping? Round up and say Stimmt so. It means 'keep the change'.
Let's run the whole scene. Waiter first, then you.
Was möchten Sie? Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee und ein Wasser, bitte. Gern!
Later. Die Rechnung, bitte. Zusammen oder getrennt? Zusammen. Mit Karte, bitte. Danke! Stimmt so.
That's a full restaurant visit. In German. You survived.

lines.quiz: How do you say: The bill, please?

lines.say: Fed and happy. Now, let's get you to the train station without getting lost.
Every question to a stranger starts with one word: Entschuldigung. Excuse me.
Long word, I know. Break it up: Ent. Schul. Di. Gung. You've got this.
Then: Wo ist, plus the place.
Now the answers. Three words and you can follow any directions.
Links. Left.
Rechts. Right.
Geradeaus. Straight ahead.
Tip: links sounds like 'links' in English, but it's left. Think: l for left. Easy.
Now, the transport. Watch the colors.
Der Bus.
Der Zug. The train.
Die U-Bahn. The subway.
Die Straßenbahn. The tram.
Das Taxi.
Buying a ticket? Die Fahrkarte. Red.
Notice: going to a city is nach. Nach Berlin. Nach Hamburg. Nach München.
Mini scene. Entschuldigung, wo ist der Bahnhof? Geradeaus und dann links. Danke! Bitte!
Und dann means 'and then'. Glue words like that make you sound natural instantly.

lines.quiz: How do you say: straight ahead?

lines.say: You made it to the station. But when does your train leave? Let's learn time.
The question: Wie spät ist es? Literally, how late is it?
The answer: Es ist, number, Uhr.
Now the one that confuses everyone. Halb vier. Half four. But it means three thirty!
Germans think: half of the way to four. So halb always looks forward to the next hour.
Quarter past? Viertel nach. Quarter to? Viertel vor.
One more thing. Trains, shops and offices use the 24-hour clock. So 2 p.m. is vierzehn Uhr. And 'at' a time is um.

lines.repeat: Der Zug kommt um vierzehn Uhr.

lines.say: Now, the days. Good news: they're all blue. Der Montag, der Dienstag. All der.
Montag, Dienstag, Mittwoch.
Donnerstag, Freitag.
And the best part of the week. Samstag, Sonntag. Das Wochenende! The weekend. That one's green.
Fun fact. Mittwoch means 'mid-week'. And Donnerstag is 'Thunder day'. Thor's day, like Thursday.
To say 'on Monday', use am. Am Montag. Am Freitag.
Three last time words: heute, morgen, gestern.

lines.quiz: How do you say: It's three thirty?

lines.say: Halb vier! If you said halb drei, you're in good company. Now, the mistakes that make Germans laugh.
First, the magic words. Bitte means please. And also 'you're welcome'. Two jobs, one word.
When you're lost in a conversation, these three lines save you.
Wait. Why Sie there, and not du? Great question.
Du is the friendly you. For friends, family, kids, and people your age at a party.
Sie, with a capital S, is the polite you. For strangers, shop staff, your boss, the police.
With Sie, the verb looks just like the infinitive. Sprechen Sie? Kommen Sie? Easy.
When in doubt, start with Sie. If they want du, they'll tell you. And they might say: Wir können uns duzen. Let's use du.
Oh, and Germans can sound very direct. It's not rude. It's just efficient. Like this video.
Now, the mistakes. Number one. It's summer, you're sweating. Do not say 'Ich bin heiß'.
That means 'I'm hot'. As in, attractive. Or, let's say, in the mood.
What you want is Mir ist heiß. Literally, 'to me, it is hot'.
Mistake number two. After a big dinner, never say 'Ich bin voll'. That means 'I'm drunk'.
Say Ich bin satt. I'm full.
Mistake three. Ich will does not mean 'I will'. It means 'I want'. And it's a bit pushy. Ich möchte is nicer.
Mistake four. Bekommen is not 'become'. It means 'to get'. So Ich bekomme ein Schnitzel just means you're getting a schnitzel. Nobody is turning into food.
And a classic: das Gift. In German, Gift means poison. So be careful what you wish for at birthdays.
A present is das Geschenk.

lines.quiz: You're sweating in the sun. What do you say?

lines.say: You just dodged the most embarrassing beginner mistakes. Now, final round. Speed quiz.
Eight questions. Three seconds each. Answer out loud before I do. Let's go!

lines.quiz: How do you say: good morning?
How do you say: My name is Tom?
How do you say: the house? Watch the color!
How do you say: Where is the train station?
How do you say: I'd like a coffee?
How do you say: I'm full, after a meal?
How do you say: See you tomorrow?

lines.say: How many did you get? Tell me your score in the comments. Eight out of eight? Write Sehr gut!
Look at you. Greetings, introductions, colors, numbers, verbs, questions, food, directions, time, and the classic mistakes. That's your A1 foundation.
Twenty-five minutes ago, this was just noise. Now you can greet, order, count, ask, and find your train. That is real progress.
Comment one German sentence about yourself. Ich heiße, ich komme aus, ich wohne in. I read them.
If this helped, subscribe to Fast German. German in seconds, not hours.
Danke fürs Zuschauen, und bis bald! Tschüss!
